title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a market prices a business at forty times trailing earnings, it is no longer paying for what the factory built yesterday—it is underwriting the next decade of execution.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk

web_blocks.html: At the NSE close of ₹7,647.50 on November 16, 2026 [28], Garware Hi-Tech Films Limited (GRWRHITECH) holds a market cap of ₹17,768 Cr across 2.323 crore shares [1]. Net of ₹933 Cr in cash and liquid funds (Sep 30, 2026) [25] and ₹13 Cr in debt [1], enterprise value is ₹16,848 Cr. Against TTM net profit of ₹426 Cr (EPS ₹183.41) and TTM operating profit of ₹547 Cr [1], the stock trades at 41.7x TTM P/E and 6.11x Price-to-Book (book value ₹1,251/share) [1]. That equals 30.8x EV/TTM Operating EBITDA, or ~27.0x EV/EBITDA including ₹77 Cr of treasury other income.

Why does the market pay 41.7x trailing earnings for a polyester film maker while domestic peers trade at 5x to 14x? Investors must separate the accounting past from the earnings inflection now underway. GRWRHITECH re-rated from a ₹2,691 52-week low [1] to a ₹8,079.50 high [28] as H1 FY27 sales jumped 25% YoY to ₹1,329 Cr and PAT surged 50% YoY to ₹262 Cr [25]. Annualizing H1 FY27 PAT (adjusting for Q3 seasonal softness and Q4 recovery [23]) points to ₹490–520 Cr in FY27E PAT. That compresses the forward multiple to 34.2x–36.3x FY27E P/E. If the Lubrizol TPU line adds 150–200 bps to FY28 margins [24] and the ₹191 Cr SCF line opens in H1 FY28 [23], FY28E PAT of ₹600–640 Cr lowers the two-year forward P/E to 27.8x–29.6x.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Implied Expectations at 2026-11-16 Close ₹7,647.50 (EV ₹16,848 Cr, WACC 11.5%, Terminal Growth 5.0%)
web_blocks.takeaway: At ₹7,647.50, the market prices in ~17.5% annual FCF compounding for a decade. Note that our ₹7,215–₹7,580 support zone still sits 27.5%–33.9% above the Conservative DCF value of ₹5,660.

web_blocks.html: Our Reverse DCF makes the risk-reward asymmetry clear. We use an 11.5% WACC (fitting an Indian mid-cap exporter with 51% US sales [2] and zero debt) and a 5.0% terminal growth rate. At ₹16,848 Cr EV, normalized free cash flow must compound at ~17.5% a year for 10 straight years. That is reachable if management hits its FY28–31 goal of ~20% sales CAGR and >27% EBITDA margins [24]. Architectural films and PDLC smart glass must also scale toward ₹1,000 Cr without hurting pricing. Yet anyone buying at ₹7,647.50 pays full fare up front. That leaves zero margin of safety if raw material costs spike or US trade rules tighten.

web_blocks.caption: Indian Polyester & Specialty Films Peer Valuation & Return Comparison (Session: 2026-11-16)
web_blocks.takeaway: GRWRHITECH trades at a steep 41.7x P/E vs. 5.2x–13.6x for packaging film peers, but earns its premium through 18.1% headline ROCE (>28% ex-cash) and 23%–28.7% OPM versus 1%–11% ROCE among commodity BOPET peers.

web_blocks.html: The peer table shows why naive P/E screens miss the divide in Indian polyester films. Commodity BOPET and BOPP peers remain stuck in global oversupply at ~54% utilization [18]. Polyplex (13.6x P/E, 0.89% ROCE), Jindal Poly Films (-1.99% ROCE, Stage 4) [19], UFlex (5.3x P/E, 7.03% ROCE), and Ester Industries (40.9x P/E, 2.75% ROCE) all struggle with low returns. Only Cosmo First (10.2x P/E, 11.2% ROCE, Stage 2) shows a cycle recovery. By contrast, GRWRHITECH earns 75% of sales from Sun Control Films (51%) and Paint Protection Films (24%) [23]. It posts 27.2%–30.3% quarterly EBITDA margins [25] and 18.1% headline ROCE (32% ex-revaluation and ex-cash [24]). Globally, asset-light XPEL, Inc. [16][17] is the closest peer. Yet GRWRHITECH captures 1,000–1,500 bps higher gross margins (54%–60% vs. 42%–45%) via chip-to-film integration [1][4][16].

web_blocks.title: Valuation Discipline: Great Business, Full Multiple at 52-Week Highs
paragraphs: At the 2026-11-16 close of ₹7,647.50, GRWRHITECH trades at 41.7x trailing earnings and ~28x–30x FY28E earnings. That supports a 12–18 month Base target of ₹9,300 (+21.6% from CMP), yet the margin of safety above Conservative DCF (₹5,660) remains thin.

web_blocks.mechanism: PPF & window film brand re-rated to 50x–70x P/E during post-COVID aftermarket boom as investors extrapolated 30%+ growth indefinitely; when US dealership attach rates normalized and China/EV OEM shifts slowed growth to single digits in 2024, the multiple compressed by >55% despite resilient gross margins.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Stock fell from $103 peak (2021) to ~$34 (2024) — a 67% drawdown while revenue still grew from $259M to ~$420M.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Even genuine PPF compounders suffer severe multiple compression when priced at 40x+ trailing P/E if top-line growth decelerates. Entry discipline at technical support matters as much as business quality.

web_blocks.html: Reconciling Accounting Book Value with Economic Value: At 6.11x Price-to-Book [1], asset-based buyers often balk at GRWRHITECH's price. Adjust equity for the ₹933 Cr net cash hoard [25], however, and the operating franchise trades at ~₹16,848 Cr EV [1]. That equals ~32x TTM operating EBITDA and ~29x–31x FY28E PAT [1][23]. Over 28% ex-cash ROCE and clear TPU/SCF catalysts support that multiple, yet CMP ₹7,647.50 leaves no cushion for a US demand dip.

Valuation Trigger: A pullback into ₹7,215–₹7,580 compresses entry valuation to ~26x–28x FY28E PAT and delivers 1.62:1 base-case asymmetry to ₹9,300 (stop ₹6,520). Conversely, a renewed US tariff hike (>25%) or Q3/Q4 FY27 EBITDA margin slip below 22% would cut fair value toward ₹6,100.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have audited the factory floor, the Lubrizol TPU partnership, the working capital nuances, and the ten-year cash ledger without looking at the ticker tape, it is time to open the market screen and ask the hardest question in investing: at ₹7,647.50 per share on November 16, 2026, what is Mr. Market already assuming about Garware Hi-Tech Films?

Let us do the arithmetic together cleanly. With 2.323 crore shares outstanding, ₹7,647.50 gives us a market capitalization of ₹17,768 crore. Subtract ₹933 crore of cash and liquid investments sitting on the September 2026 balance sheet and add back the ₹13 crore of short-term borrowings, and you arrive at an enterprise value of ₹16,848 crore. Against trailing twelve-month net profit of ₹426 crore and operating EBITDA of ₹547 crore, the market is asking us to pay 41.7 times trailing earnings and 30.8 times trailing operating EBITDA.

If you only looked at Indian packaging film peers—Polyplex at 13.6 times earnings, UFlex at 5.2 times, Cosmo First at 9.9 times, or Jindal Poly losing money—41.7 times would look absurd. Why would anyone pay four times the sector multiple for a company in Aurangabad that starts with polyester chips? The answer lies in the structural chasm we uncovered in Chapters 2 and 6. Those peers are fighting for survival in a global BOPET commodity glut running at 54% capacity utilization, earning 1% to 11% ROCE. Garware has quietly vacated the commodity battlefield: 75% of its Q2 FY27 revenue came from Sun Control Films and Paint Protection Films, driving a 28.7% H1 FY27 EBITDA margin and an ex-cash, ex-revaluation ROCE north of 28%.

Yet acknowledging that Garware deserves a premium multiple does not absolve us from checking what ₹7,647.50 bakes into the cake. When we run a Reverse DCF on ₹16,848 crore of enterprise value using an 11.5% discount rate and a 5% terminal growth rate, the math tells a sobering story: to justify ₹7,647.50 today, normalized free cash flow must compound at roughly 17.5% every single year for the next decade while sustaining 27.5% to 28.5% EBITDA margins.

Can Garware deliver that? Looking at H1 FY27—where revenue grew 25% to ₹1,329 crore and PAT surged 50% to ₹262 crore—the near-term earnings bridge is certainly visible. If FY27 finishes near ₹500 crore of PAT and the Q3 FY27 TPU line plus H1 FY28 automated SCF line lift FY28 PAT toward ₹620 crore, the two-year forward P/E compresses from 41.7x down to roughly 30x. But notice the catch: if you buy right here at ₹7,647.50, just 1.4% below the 52-week high of ₹8,079.50, you are paying for that entire FY27–FY28 operational ramp before a single roll of TPU film has cleared commercial customer qualification. Think of XPEL in the United States between 2021 and 2024: an undisputed PPF category leader whose stock still fell 67% from $103 to $34 when its 50x+ multiple met a cyclical slowdown. At 41.7x trailing earnings, Garware is priced for execution perfection—which is precisely why our next step is to read the technical tape for a disciplined entry zone rather than chasing strength.

Let us also test one more angle on valuation before we leave Chapter 7: what happens to the multiple if our Base Case plays out over the next eighteen months? Suppose Garware delivers ₹2,600 crore of revenue in FY27 at a 27% EBITDA margin and then ramps the Lubrizol TPU line plus the automated SCF line in FY28, lifting FY28 revenue toward ₹3,050 crore and PAT toward ₹620–₹640 crore (roughly ₹270–₹275 EPS). Even if the market multiple compresses from 41.7x trailing P/E down to 33.8x—which is a realistic steady-state multiple for a 20%-growing, debt-free specialty materials leader—the stock would trade at ₹9,300.

Notice the asymmetry math in that projection: from today's ₹7,647.50, ₹9,300 is +21.6% upside against -17.5% risk to our ₹6,520 invalidation stop—a sub-par 0.92:1 to 1.33:1 trade. From our ₹7,215–₹7,580 support zone, however, ₹9,300 is +22.7% to +28.9% upside against -9.6% to -14.0% risk, giving us an earned 1.62:1 reward-to-risk ratio.

That distinction between operating earnings and treasury income is where disciplined institutional valuation separates itself from surface-level screening. Even after crediting the ₹933 crore cash pile at full face value, an investor paying ₹7,647.50 today is still paying ₹16,848 crore for the operating enterprise—nearly 32 times trailing operating EBITDA.

Nothing in our Reverse DCF says Garware cannot grow into that valuation over the next three to five years. If TPU backward integration adds 150–200 bps to margins and architectural films scale toward ₹1,000 crore, the earnings power will be substantial. What the Reverse DCF insists upon is humility: at 41.7x trailing P/E, the market has already awarded Garware full credit for execution, leaving zero room for an unforced error.

In short, our Reverse DCF and peer comparison leave us with a nuanced but actionable conclusion: Garware's 41.7x trailing P/E is earned relative to commodity BOPET peers trading at 5x–14x with single-digit ROCE, yet it leaves no valuation cushion at ₹7,647.50. Letting the price come back toward ₹7,215–₹7,580 improves our entry multiple to ~39x–41x trailing and ~26x–28x FY28E earnings.

Always anchor your valuation expectations to what can go wrong as well as what can go right. At ₹7,647.50, Garware is priced for 17.5% annual free cash flow growth over ten years. That is achievable if TPU integration and architectural films fire on schedule, but it leaves no room for a US customer loss or margin compression.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hardest discipline in quality investing is separating 'great business' from 'great entry price.' At 41.7x TTM P/E and 1.4% below its 52-week high, Garware Hi-Tech Films is pricing in ~18% annual FCF compounding for ten years. We want to own this engine—but on our terms, at a pullback to institutional support, not after a 4.2% single-day spike.
